metadata.name: uptime
metadata.displayName: uptime - Show how long system has been running
metadata.description: Show how long system has been running and system load

installation.note: uptime is typically included in procps package, available on most Linux systems by default

overview.summary: The uptime command displays how long the system has been running, the current time, number of logged-in users, and system load averages. It's a quick way to check system status and see if the system is under heavy load.
when_to_use: Check how long system has been running

syntax.description: Display system uptime and load information. No arguments needed - just run 'uptime'.

options.use_case: Get uptime in easy-to-read format like '2 days, 3 hours'
See when the system was last booted

examples.title: Basic uptime information
examples.description: Display system uptime and load averages

output_explanation.format: Time, uptime, users, and load averages

elements.meaning: System has been running for 5 days, 3 hours, 15 minutes
Number of users currently logged in
System load averages for 1, 5, and 15 minutes (lower is better, 1.0 = fully loaded on single-core)

output_explanation.notes: Load average shows system activity. On a single-core system, 1.0 means fully utilized. On multi-core, divide by number of cores.

examples.title: Pretty format

output_explanation.notes: The -p flag provides a cleaner, more readable format without the time and load information.

examples.use_case: Get uptime in readable format for scripts or display

examples.title: System boot time
examples.description: Show when the system was last booted

elements.meaning: Exact date and time when system was booted

output_explanation.notes: Useful for knowing when the system was last restarted, helpful for troubleshooting or maintenance records.

examples.use_case: Check when system was last rebooted

misconceptions.title: Load average of 1.0 means system is overloaded
misconceptions.misconception: A load average of 1.0 always means the system is fully loaded
misconceptions.reality: On a single-core system, 1.0 means fully utilized. On a 4-core system, 1.0 means only 25% utilized. Load average should be compared to number of CPU cores.
misconceptions.tip: Divide load average by number of CPU cores to understand utilization. Use 'nproc' to see CPU count.

misconceptions.title: Uptime shows application uptime
misconceptions.misconception: uptime shows how long a specific application has been running
misconceptions.reality: uptime shows system (OS) uptime, not application uptime. Use 'ps' or application-specific commands for application uptime.
misconceptions.tip: uptime is for system-level information. For application uptime, check the application's status or logs.

common_pitfalls.description: Not considering number of CPU cores when reading load averages
common_pitfalls.solution: Compare load average to number of CPU cores. Load of 4.0 on 4-core system = fully utilized, load of 4.0 on 1-core system = overloaded

common_pitfalls.issue: High load doesn't always mean problem
common_pitfalls.description: High load average might be normal for the system's workload
common_pitfalls.solution: Understand your system's normal load patterns. Temporary spikes are normal, sustained high load may indicate issues

related_commands.relationship: System monitoring; top shows detailed process info, uptime shows summary
Interactive monitoring; htop shows detailed system info, uptime shows quick summary
User information; w shows logged-in users and their activity, uptime shows user count
related_commands.description: Show who is logged on and what they are doing

best_practices: Use uptime for quick system status checks
Use -p for readable uptime in scripts or reports
Use -s to check when system was last rebooted
Monitor load averages over time to understand normal patterns
Compare load averages to CPU core count for accurate interpretation
performance_tips: uptime is very fast - negligible performance impact
Load averages are calculated by the kernel, so uptime just displays them
Use uptime in monitoring scripts for lightweight system checks

additional_notes.load_average: Shows average system load over 1, 5, and 15 minutes. Lower is better. Compare to CPU core count.
additional_notes.uptime_accuracy: Uptime is accurate to the second and is maintained by the kernel
additional_notes.user_count: Shows number of distinct user sessions, not individual users
additional_notes.system_health: Regular uptime checks help identify if system needs maintenance or reboot
